blueprint.title: Query Plan Histogram Regression
blueprint.scenario: An open-source analytics database ships a compiled query-execution engine (`/usr/local/bin/qengine`) that accepts SQLite-dialect queries over CSV files. A regression was filed: aggregate histogram queries that worked in v1.1 now return wrong bucket counts on certain inputs. The repo contains a thin Python shim (`/app/runner.py`) that normalises queries and feeds them to the binary, plus a sample dataset and a few passing smoke tests. The binary has no source available in the container.
blueprint.instruction_draft: The query engine at `/usr/local/bin/qengine` produces incorrect results for WIDTH_BUCKET histogram aggregations. Fix `/app/runner.py` so that every WIDTH_BUCKET query returns counts that match the mathematical definition: each value v is placed in bucket ceil((v - lo) / w) clamped to [1, n], where w = (hi - lo) / n, lo and hi are the declared bounds, and n is the bucket count; values equal to hi fall in bucket n, values outside [lo, hi] are excluded. The engine itself must not be replaced or patched.
requirements: WIDTH_BUCKET(v, lo, hi, n) places v in bucket floor((v - lo) / w) + 1 where w = (hi - lo) / n, clamped to [1, n]
Values exactly equal to hi are placed in bucket n (not excluded)
Values strictly less than lo or strictly greater than hi are excluded from all buckets
Bucket counts must be exact integers; no rounding error propagation
The runner must invoke qengine for the actual SQL evaluation; it cannot reimplement the full SQL engine
Queries with non-uniform data distributions (skewed, repeated boundary values, floats near bucket edges) must return correct counts
environment: Compile a C binary /usr/local/bin/qengine that wraps SQLite's execution but rewires WIDTH_BUCKET with TWO deliberate bugs: (1) boundary bug — values == hi are excluded (treated as > hi) instead of placed in bucket n; (2) floating-point accumulation bug — bucket width w is computed as integer division (lo and hi cast to int before subtracting) so fractional ranges are truncated, misplacing values near bucket edges
The binary accepts: qengine '<SQL>' '<csv_path>' and prints tab-separated rows
SQL dialect: SELECT col, WIDTH_BUCKET(val_col, lo_lit, hi_lit, n_lit) AS bucket, COUNT(*) FROM t GROUP BY bucket ORDER BY bucket
The runner /app/runner.py currently passes the query verbatim to qengine — it is about 120 lines with CSV loading, query parsing, and output formatting
/app/data/sample.csv: 50 rows of (id, value) with values in [0.0, 100.0], smoke tests pass on this file
/app/tests/smoke.py: 3 tests using sample.csv that all pass with the buggy binary because the sample avoids hi-boundary values and uses integer-aligned ranges
/app/README.md: documents the WIDTH_BUCKET contract including the hi-inclusive rule and the floating-point formula
~1500 lines total across runner, a query parser module, a CSV schema inferencer, output formatters, and unrelated aggregation helpers (SUM, AVG, MEDIAN)
blueprint.internal_hint: Two interacting bugs live in the compiled qengine binary: (1) boundary exclusion — v==hi is dropped instead of mapped to bucket n; (2) integer-truncation of w — the C code computes w as (int)(hi-lo)/(double)n instead of (double)(hi-lo)/n, so for non-integer ranges the bucket width is wrong. Bug 1 is easy to spot by probing the binary with boundary values. Bug 2 only manifests with fractional (lo,hi) spans and causes misclassification of values near bucket edges — fixing bug 1 alone passes the smoke tests and many hand-crafted checks. The solver must intercept WIDTH_BUCKET calls in runner.py, rewrite them to push the full computation into SQLite expressions that the binary evaluates correctly (using CAST and CASE expressions), effectively pre-computing bucket assignment in the rewritten SQL rather than relying on qengine's native WIDTH_BUCKET implementation. The correct rewrite is: CASE WHEN v < lo OR v > hi THEN NULL ELSE MIN(n, CAST(FLOOR((CAST(v AS REAL) - lo) / ((CAST(hi AS REAL) - CAST(lo AS REAL)) / n)) + 1 AS INTEGER)) END. The solver discovers this only by running experiments: probing with boundary values (finds bug 1), then probing with fractional ranges like WIDTH_BUCKET(x, 0.0, 3.0, 3) on values {0.5, 1.0, 1.5} (finds bug 2). The sample data uses integer boundaries [0,100] so bug 2 is invisible there.
blueprint.trap: A solver that only fixes the hi-boundary case (adds a CASE WHEN v = hi THEN n) passes all smoke tests and passes spot checks with integer ranges, but fails the hidden corpus which includes fractional (lo, hi) spans and values near non-integer bucket edges. The integer-truncation bug shifts entire buckets for any range where (hi-lo) is not an integer multiple of n, which is common in real data.
tests: Boundary corpus: generate 200 queries at verify time with values exactly equal to hi; every such value must appear in bucket n
Fractional-range corpus: generate 300 queries with lo/hi as non-integer floats (e.g. lo=0.7, hi=5.3, n=4); compare bucket assignments against a reference Python implementation of the spec formula
Edge-cluster corpus: generate 150 queries with many values clustered within 1e-9 of bucket boundaries; counts must match reference within 0 tolerance (exact integer match)
Exclusion corpus: generate 100 queries with values outside [lo, hi]; verify those rows are absent from output
Mixed corpus: 50 queries mixing in-range, boundary-equal, and out-of-range values in the same dataset; full count vector must match reference
Adversarial: n=1 (single bucket), n=100 (fine), lo==hi-epsilon (very narrow range), negative lo; all must match spec

verifier_knob.name: corpus_size
verifier_knob.effect: Halving corpus_size (400) makes it easier to get lucky with a partial fix; doubling (1600) with more fractional edge cases makes even careful fixes fail if the formula has off-by-epsilon issues

expected_failure_modes: Solver fixes only the hi-boundary bug, passes smoke + boundary corpus, fails fractional-range corpus
Solver patches the binary with a hex editor or replaces it entirely rather than fixing runner.py as required
Solver reimplements WIDTH_BUCKET in Python in runner.py but with a wrong formula (e.g. uses round instead of floor, or mishandles the CAST order)
Solver constructs a SQL rewrite that passes integer-range tests but uses integer division internally, reproducing bug 2 in the rewrite
Solver does not discover bug 2 because they test only with the provided sample.csv which has integer bounds

invalid_failure_risks: GCC may optimize away the intentional integer-truncation bug depending on version/flags, making bug 2 absent or inconsistent in the compiled binary

Formula inconsistency: instruction draft says 'ceil((v-lo)/w)' but requirements say 'floor((v-lo)/w)+1'; these differ when (v-lo)/w is exactly an integer (boundary cluster values), potentially making edge-cluster corpus tests ambiguous or wrong

Implementing a reliable SQLite extension binary that parses WIDTH_BUCKET as a custom SQL function is non-trivial C; subtle parsing or aggregation bugs in the build could cause flakiness unrelated to the intended bugs
The WIDTH_BUCKET regex interceptor in runner.py may fail on whitespace variants, quoted identifiers, or subexpressions, causing false failures unrelated to the solver's fix logic

Smoke tests passing 'because sample avoids hi-boundary values and uses integer-aligned ranges' is fragile — if sample.csv generation is not precisely controlled, smoke tests could accidentally trigger the bugs and fail before any fix
review.reasons: genuine_difficulty scores 2 because a skilled agent can discover both bugs in ~5 probe commands and implement the correct SQL CASE/CAST rewrite directly from the spec formula in ~15 total commands — the README documents the exact formula, making the fix essentially transcription work. The formula inconsistency between 'ceil' and 'floor+1' in the instruction creates an ambiguous edge case at exact integer bucket boundaries that could invalidate some edge-cluster corpus tests. The intentional C integer-truncation bug is fragile to reproduce reliably across GCC versions without carefully pinned flags.
fixes: Raise genuine difficulty: hide the formula from README (document only the English rule 'each value placed in a bucket proportional to its distance from lo'), forcing the solver to derive the correct formula by experimentation and cross-checking against a spec they must infer

Add a third interacting bug (e.g., off-by-one in GROUP BY bucket ordering or NULL handling in the aggregation) so that fixing the SQL rewrite still requires understanding the binary's output format peculiarities

Resolve the ceil/floor+1 inconsistency: pick one canonical form throughout instruction, requirements, and test reference implementation, and add an explicit note about behavior when (v-lo)/w is exactly an integer

Pin the GCC version and add explicit compilation flags (-O0 -fno-optimize-sibling-calls) and a build-time test that verifies both bugs are present in the compiled binary before the container is sealed
Make the smoke tests use fractional ranges so they cannot be passed by fixing only bug 1, eliminating the shallow-fix trap and forcing solvers to find both bugs before they even see the hidden corpus

verdicts.reason: Completely different domain: HTTP server with primality testing vs. fixing a Python shim to correctly implement WIDTH_BUCKET histogram semantics around a closed-source binary.
That task is about query performance optimization for correctness-preserving rewrites in PostgreSQL, not about patching a Python wrapper to fix bucket-boundary semantics for a closed-source binary.
Entirely different domain: probabilistic graphical model learning and inference vs. fixing histogram bucket logic in a Python shim.

Both tasks involve characterizing and working around a closed-source binary by fixing a surrounding Python/shell pipeline to produce mathematically correct output, with no source patching of the binary allowed; the core challenge and approach are essentially the same.

That task is about repairing a Rust NetFlow aggregation service with UDP/TCP networking bugs, which is a fundamentally different problem from patching a Python query shim for histogram bucket correctness.
